claim: Soluble karyopherins of the importin-β (impβ) family use RanGTP to transport cargos directionally through the nuclear pore complex (NPC).
source: Soluble karyopherins of the importin-β (impβ) family use RanGTP to transport cargos directionally through the nuclear pore complex (NPC).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of nuclear transport, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: A stable pool of impβ exists at the NPC.
source: In this study, we identify a stable pool of impβ at the NPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FRAP and photo-conversion experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: A subpopulation of the stable impβ pool is rapidly turned-over by RanGTP, likely at Nup153.
source: A subpopulation of this pool is rapidly turned-over by RanGTP, likely at Nup153.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data showing rapid turnover with RanGTP (Figure 1D), dSTORM data showing depletion at the nuclear face (Figure 3), and photobleach counting data (Figure 4).

claim: Impβ, but not transportin-1 (TRN1), alters the pore's permeability in a Ran-dependent manner.
source: Impβ, but not transportin-1 (TRN1), alters the pore's permeability in a Ran-dependent manner, suggesting that impβ is a functional component of the NPC.
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assays with GFP probes showing that impβ restricts permeability while TRN1 does not (Figure 5C-E).

claim: Upon reduction of Nup153 levels, inert cargos more readily equilibrate across the NPC yet active transport is impaired.
source: Upon reduction of Nup153 levels, inert cargos more readily equilibrate across the NPC yet active transport is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased passive equilibration but decreased active transport in Nup153 knockdown cells (Figure 5A,B).

claim: When purified impβ or TRN1 are mixed with Nup153 in vitro, higher-order, multivalent complexes form.
source: When purified impβ or TRN1 are mixed with Nup153 in vitro, higher-order, multivalent complexes form.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data showing large intensity bursts indicative of complex formation (Figure 6B-D).

claim: RanGTP dissolves the impβ•Nup153 complexes but not those of TRN1•Nup153.
source: RanGTP dissolves the impβ•Nup153 complexes but not those of TRN1•Nup153.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy showing that RanQ69L•GTP prevents and dissolves impβ•Nup153FG complexes but not TRN1•Nup153FG complexes (Figure 6).

claim: Impβ and Nup153 interact at the NPC's nuclear face to form a Ran-regulated mesh that modulates NPC permeability.
source: We propose that impβ and Nup153 interact at the NPC's nuclear face to form a Ran-regulated mesh that modulates NPC permeability.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of multiple experimental findings including dSTORM localization, permeability assays, and in vitro complex formation.

claim: The NPC controls the nuclear entry and exit of cargos ranging from single proteins to large ribonucleoprotein complexes.
source: The NPC controls the nuclear entry and exit of cargos ranging from single proteins to large ribonucleoprotein complexes (Stewart, 2007; Peters, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Cargos smaller than ∼40 kDa can passively equilibrate across the nuclear envelope.
source: Cargos smaller than ∼40 kDa can passively equilibrate across the nuclear envelope while larger cargos must bind special transport receptors to move from the cytoplasm into the nucleus and accumulate there (Stewart, 2007; Peters, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Larger cargos must bind special transport receptors to move from the cytoplasm into the nucleus and accumulate there.
source: Cargos smaller than ∼40 kDa can passively equilibrate across the nuclear envelope while larger cargos must bind special transport receptors to move from the cytoplasm into the nucleus and accumulate there (Stewart, 2007; Peters, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Transport receptors can bind cargos and interact with unstructured phenylalanine–glycine repeat proteins (FG nucleoporins) within the pore.
source: These transport receptors are able to bind cargos but can also interact with unstructured phenylalanine–glycine repeat proteins (FG nucleoporins) within the pore.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of nuclear transport.

claim: Directional transport of cargos is powered by the small GTPase Ran and a system of compartment-specific GTP hydrolysis and GDP-to-GTP exchange.
source: Directional transport of cargos is powered by the small GTPase Ran and a system of compartment-specific GTP hydrolysis and GDP-to-GTP exchange, which establishes a sharp concentration gradient of RanGTP across the nuclear envelope (Izaurralde et al., 1997; Kalab et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The Ran system establishes a sharp concentration gradient of RanGTP across the nuclear envelope.
source: Directional transport of cargos is powered by the small GTPase Ran and a system of compartment-specific GTP hydrolysis and GDP-to-GTP exchange, which establishes a sharp concentration gradient of RanGTP across the nuclear envelope (Izaurralde et al., 1997; Kalab et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Importin-β and other members of the karyopherin family form a complex with their cognate cargos in the RanGTP-low cytoplasmic environment.
source: Importin-β (impβ) and other members of the karyopherin family of nuclear transport receptors form a complex with their cognate cargos in the RanGTP-low cytoplasmic environment and release cargos upon binding to RanGTP in the nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of nuclear transport.

claim: Importin-β releases cargos upon binding to RanGTP in the nucleus.
source: Importin-β (impβ) and other members of the karyopherin family of nuclear transport receptors form a complex with their cognate cargos in the RanGTP-low cytoplasmic environment and release cargos upon binding to RanGTP in the nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of nuclear transport.

claim: Early studies suggested that Ran is needed for cargos to move through the NPC.
source: First, early studies have suggested that Ran is needed for cargos to move through the NPC (Moore and Blobel, 1993; Gorlich et al., 1994; Moore and Blobel, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ran plays an important role in dissociating impβ from the nuclear face of the NPC, in addition to displacing impβ from cargos.
source: Second, it was shown that Ran plays an important role in dissociating impβ from the nuclear face of the NPC, in addition to displacing impβ from cargos (Gorlich et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Without RanGTP, cargos entered the pore but had an ∼100-fold higher probability of exiting the pore at the cytoplasmic face than the nuclear face.
source: Without RanGTP, cargos entered the pore but had an ∼100-fold higher probability of exiting the pore at the cytoplasmic face than the nuclear face, suggesting that RanGTP influences barriers felt by cargo-impβ complexes within the pore (Lowe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Ran-sensitive exit asymmetry of large cargo-receptor complexes suggests that a Ran-dependent process takes place inside the channel near the nuclear face of the pore at about ∼70 nm along the transport axis.
source: The Ran-sensitive exit asymmetry of large cargo-receptor complexes suggests that a currently unexplained Ran-dependent process takes place inside the channel near the nuclear face of the pore at about ∼70 nm along the transport axis (Lowe et al., 2010) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The overall transport success of large cargos appears to be more sensitive to RanGTP levels than other cargos.
source: Fourth, the overall transport success of large cargos appears to be more sensitive to RanGTP levels than other cargos (Lyman et al., 2002; Snow et al., 2013) and thus RanGTP somehow influences the interplay of cargo size and active transport.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RanGTP influences the interplay of cargo size and active transport.
source: Fourth, the overall transport success of large cargos appears to be more sensitive to RanGTP levels than other cargos (Lyman et al., 2002; Snow et al., 2013) and thus RanGTP somehow influences the interplay of cargo size and active transport.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: The connection between cargo size sensitivity and RanGTP is not necessarily mediated by cargo multivalency.
source: This latter connection is not necessarily mediated by cargo multivalency (Snow et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SA-IBB4 strongly stains the nuclear envelope but does not efficiently enter the nuclear interior in the presence of physiological levels of impβ without RanGTP.
source: In the presence of physiological levels of impβ (1 μM, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), SA-IBB4 strongly stains the nuclear envelope but does not efficiently enter the nuclear interior (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Cargo molecules accumulate within the NPC due to their inability to complete their translocation into the nucleus in the absence of Ran.
source: This indicates that cargo molecules accumulate within the NPC, presumably due to their inability to complete their translocation into the nucleus in the absence of Ran.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cargos stain the nuclear envelope but do not enter the nucleus.

claim: When RanGDP + GTP is added, the fluorescence intensity of the nuclear rim drops while that of the nuclear interior increases.
source: However, when RanGDP (5 μM) + GTP (2 mM) (henceforth referred to as RanGTP) is added, the fluorescence intensity of the nuclear rim drops while that of the nuclear interior increases, showing that the cargos then efficiently exit the NPC and accumulate in the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Impβ-YFP formed a bright nuclear rim when added without RanGTP.
source: As expected for a FG-binding karyopherin, impβ-YFP formed a bright nuclear rim when added without RanGTP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The impβ-YFP signal at the rim was substantially reduced but not completely eliminated by RanGTP.
source: However, as with the SA-IBB4 cargos, the impβ-YFP signal at the rim was substantially reduced but not completely eliminated by RanGTP (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Ran modulates the way in which the NPC interacts with both cargo-bound impβ and free impβ.
source: Ran thus modulates the way in which the NPC interacts with both cargo-bound impβ and free impβ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RanGTP reduces rim fluorescence for both cargo-impβ complexes and free impβ.

claim: At least a subset of non-cargo engaged but NPC-bound transport receptors must be RanGTP-sensitive.
source: Moreover, since RanGTP reduces the impβ-YFP rim fluorescence, at least a subset of non-cargo engaged but NPC-bound transport receptors must be RanGTP-sensitive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that free impβ-YFP rim signal is reduced by RanGTP.

claim: In the absence of RanGTP, the initial recovery of the impβ signal after bleaching took several seconds (time to 20% recovery = 1.6 ± 0.1 s).
source: In the absence of RanGTP, the initial recovery of the impβ signal after bleaching took several seconds (time to 20% recovery = 1.6 ± 0.1 s, N = 20, Figure 1D, blue).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: With RanGTP, the initial recovery was 16-fold more rapid (time to 20% recovery = 0.1 ± 0.1 s).
source: However, with RanGTP, the initial recovery was 16-fold more rapid (time to 20% recovery = 0.1 ± 0.1 s, N = 20, Figure 1D, red).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RanGTP is able to accelerate the cargo-independent turnover of impβ bound to the NPC.
source: Therefore, as already indicated by the simple rim fluorescence experiments, RanGTP is able to accelerate the cargo-independent turnover of impβ bound to the NPC.
evidence: This is an inference based on FRAP data showing faster recovery with RanGTP.

claim: Previous single-molecule titration experiments have suggested the presence of two types of impβ binding sites within the NPC.
source: Consistent with this, previous single-molecule titration experiments have suggested the presence of two types of impβ binding sites within the NPC (Tokunaga et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the absence of RanGTP, the photo-converted (red) impβ-mEos2 signal decayed to half its initial value within 3–4 min.
source: In the absence of RanGTP, the photo-converted (red) impβ-mEos2 signal decayed to half its initial value within 3–4 min (Figure 1E), showing that some impβ molecules remain at the pore for long times.
evidence: This is supported by photo-conversion experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the presence of RanGTP, the initial red signal was lower than without RanGTP (∼50 AU vs ∼75 AU).
source: In the presence of RanGTP, the initial red signal was lower than without RanGTP (∼50 AU vs ∼75 AU), consistent with the previously detected RanGTP-dependent rapid turnover of impβ within the pore.
evidence: This is supported by photo-conversion experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Some impβ molecules remained at the pore for several minutes, even in the presence of RanGTP.
source: Strikingly, however, some impβ molecules remained at the pore for several minutes, even in the presence of RanGTP (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by photo-conversion experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There are at least two pools of impβ within the NPC.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that there are at least two pools of impβ within the NPC.
evidence: This is an inference based on FRAP and photo-conversion data showing different turnover kinetics.

claim: One pool of impβ is stably bound to the NPC for many minutes, with and without RanGTP.
source: One pool is stably bound to the NPC for many minutes, with and without RanGTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on photo-conversion data showing long-lived impβ signal.

claim: The other pool of impβ is stably bound to the NPC only in the absence of RanGTP.
source: The other pool is stably bound to the NPC only in the absence of RanGTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on FRAP and photo-conversion data showing RanGTP-sensitive turnover.

claim: The mean spatial precision of dSTORM imaging was 12 nm.
source: We directly imaged and localized individual Cy5 or Alexa647 dye-labeled impβ molecules within the pore using dSTORM super-resolution localization microscopy (Heilemann et al., 2008; van de Linde et al., 2011) (Figure 2A–D; mean spatial precision, σx,y of 12 nm, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dSTORM images taken at the equatorial plane of the nucleus show discrete elongated structures oriented normal to the nuclear envelope.
source: The dSTORM images taken at the equatorial plane of the nucleus show discrete elongated structures oriented normal to the nuclear envelope (Figure 2B,E).
evidence: This is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 2B,E.

claim: Viewed from the bottom of the nucleus, radially symmetric, punctate NPC structures are observed.
source: Viewed from the bottom of the nucleus, we observe radially symmetric, punctate NPC structures (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There are two pools of impβ localizations separated by approximately 90 nm.
source: Viewed along the transport axis, there are two pools of impβ localizations separated by approximately 90 nm and occupying a footprint and spatial arrangement consistent with structural studies (Frenkiel-Krispin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 3A and is consistent with cited structural studies.

claim: The central channel measured ∼50 nm at the narrowest point.
source: The central channel measured ∼50 nm at the narrowest point, consistent with single quantum dot transport studies (Lowe et al., 2010) and other super-resolution measurements (Loschberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by dSTORM data and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: The addition of RanGTP markedly decreased the total number of impβ localizations.
source: The addition of RanGTP, which produces a transport-competent pore with active impβ turnover, markedly decreased the total number of impβ localizations (Figure 3A, 'RanGTP' and Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 3) but also changed the shape of the probability density function (PDF) of impβ molecules within the pore.
evidence: This is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplements 1, 3.

claim: In the presence of RanGTP, the PDF is bimodal and shows a depletion of impβ from the nucleoplasmic face of the NPC.
source: In the presence of RanGTP, the PDF is bimodal and shows a depletion of impβ from the nucleoplasmic face of the NPC (Figure 3C, compare red trace to black trace).
evidence: This is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RanGTP was not simply displacing impβ from the pore but was displacing impβ preferentially from specific sites within the pore.
source: RanGTP was therefore not simply displacing impβ from the pore but was displacing impβ preferentially from specific sites within the pore.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that RanGTP changes the spatial distribution of impβ within the pore.

claim: Both addition of RanGTP and reduction of Nup153 alter the arrangement and loading of impβ within the pore, especially towards the NPC's nuclear face.
source: Therefore, both addition of RanGTP and reduction of Nup153 alter the arrangement and loading of impβ within the pore, especially towards the NPC's nuclear face.
evidence: This is an inference based on dSTORM imaging data showing changes in impβ distribution.

claim: There is considerable pore-to-pore heterogeneity in the axial distribution of impβ in all studied conditions.
source: As can be seen, there is considerable pore-to-pore heterogeneity in the axial distribution of impβ in all studied conditions.
evidence: This is supported by waterfall plots shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When Nup153 was reduced, there were very few pores with a dominant impβ signal at the nuclear face.
source: The most notable difference was that when Nup153 was reduced, there were very few pores with a dominant impβ signal at the nuclear face.
evidence: This is supported by waterfall plots shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Wild type NPCs in the absence of RanGTP contained the greatest number of impβ molecules (70 bleach steps counted).
source: Wild type NPCs in the absence of RanGTP contained the greatest number of impβ molecules (70 bleach steps counted), whereas RanGTP caused a 27% decrease in impβ levels (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by photobleach step-counting data shown in Figure 4.

claim: RanGTP caused a 27% decrease in impβ levels.
source: Wild type NPCs in the absence of RanGTP contained the greatest number of impβ molecules (70 bleach steps counted), whereas RanGTP caused a 27% decrease in impβ levels (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by photobleach step-counting data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In Δ15370% nuclei, there was a 34% drop in the amount of impβ per pore without RanGTP and a 33% drop with RanGTP.
source: In Δ15370% nuclei, we found a 34% drop in the amount of impβ per pore without RanGTP and a 33% drop with RanGTP.
evidence: This is supported by photobleach step-counting data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Most of the impβ molecules that are displaced from the NPC by nuclear RanGTP are those that are bound to Nup153.
source: These results suggest that most of the impβ molecules that are displaced from the NPC by nuclear RanGTP are those that are bound to Nup153.
evidence: This is an inference based on photobleach counting data comparing wild type and Nup153 knockdown conditions.

claim: Little cargo was able to enter the nucleus under conditions of passive equilibration (i.e., in the absence of RanGTP) in wild-type cells.
source: As shown earlier (Figure 1), little cargo was able to enter the nucleus under conditions of passive equilibration (i.e., in the absence of RanGTP) in wild-type cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The cargo translocated the NPC faster in Δ15370% nuclei, indicating that the transport channel had become leakier to large cargos.
source: In contrast, the cargo translocated the NPC faster in Δ15370% nuclei, indicating that the transport channel had become leakier to large cargos and translocation became less dependent on the presence of RanGTP (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Net nuclear cargo accumulation was reduced for Δ15370% nuclei under active transport conditions.
source: Interestingly, the opposite was observed for active transport in the presence of RanGTP, where net nuclear cargo accumulation was reduced for Δ15370% nuclei (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Nup153 affects both the ease of passive impβ-mediated movement of large cargos through the pore and the efficiency of active transport into the nucleus.
source: The nucleoporin Nup153 therefore affects both the ease of passive impβ-mediated movement of large cargos through the pore and the efficiency of active transport into the nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing effects of Nup153 knockdown on both passive and active transport.

claim: 1 μM impβ significantly decreased the permeability of the NPC for the GFP1 and GFP2 probes.
source: We found that 1 μM impβ significantly decreased the permeability of the NPC for the GFP1 and GFP2 probes (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: When RanGTP was also added, the permeability was greatly increased.
source: By contrast, when RanGTP was also added, the permeability was greatly increased.
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The GFP3 probe translocated across the NPC at a relatively slow rate with or without impβ and RanGTP, likely because GFP3's size is considerably larger than the passive diffusion size cutoff of the pore.
source: The GFP3 probe translocated across the NPC at a relatively slow rate with or without impβ and RanGTP, likely because GFP3's size is considerably larger than the passive diffusion size cutoff of the pore (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5C and represents an inference about the reason for slow translocation.

claim: At 1 and even 2 μM TRN1, there was no strong effect on NPC permeability.
source: At 1 and even 2 μM TRN1, there was no strong effect on NPC permeability (Figure 5E), suggesting that general molecular crowding is not responsible for the changes to NPC permeability.
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: General molecular crowding is not responsible for the changes to NPC permeability.
source: At 1 and even 2 μM TRN1, there was no strong effect on NPC permeability (Figure 5E), suggesting that general molecular crowding is not responsible for the changes to NPC permeability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TRN1 does not affect permeability like impβ does.

claim: For Δ15370% nuclei, addition of impβ no longer restricted the NPC.
source: Importantly, for Δ15370% nuclei, addition of impβ no longer restricted the NPC (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Specifically the impβ•Nup153 interaction causes the nuclear pore to become less permeable.
source: Together, these results suggest that specifically the impβ•Nup153 interaction causes the nuclear pore to become less permeable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that impβ restricts permeability in wild type but not in Nup153 knockdown cells.

claim: The reduced permeability must be due to a specific steric 'barrier' within the pore and not due to a block of transport receptor-specific binding sites.
source: Furthermore, because the inert probes undergo purely passive translocation across the NPC, the reduced permeability must be due to a specific steric 'barrier' within the pore and not due to a block of transport receptor-specific binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that inert probes (which do not bind impβ) are affected by impβ presence.

claim: This steric barrier appears to involve impβ•Nup153 interactions that are very stable and long-lived in the absence of RanGTP.
source: This steric barrier appears to involve impβ•Nup153 interactions that are very stable and long-lived in the absence of RanGTP.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations including FRAP, photo-conversion, and permeability assays.

claim: RanGTP causes the pore to become more permeable even when no exogenous impβ is first added.
source: Indeed RanGTP causes the pore to become more permeable even when no exogenous impβ is first added.
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: This is likely due to endogenous impβ and other transport receptors residing in the pore that were not washed away during digitonin permeabilization.
source: This is likely due to endogenous impβ and other transport receptors residing in the pore that were not washed away during digitonin permeabilization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Impβ could be considered a bona fide functional component of the pore and not only a soluble transport receptor.
source: Along with the observation that impβ can persist in the pore for minutes or tens of minutes, these functional studies suggest that impβ could be considered a bona fide functional component of the pore and not only a soluble transport receptor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the long residence time and functional effects of impβ on pore permeability.

claim: The impβ•Nup153 interaction may be responsible for the permeability differences detected in inert probe passive diffusion assays and may contribute to the permeability barrier function of the NPC.
source: Moreover, the impβ•Nup153 interaction may be responsible for the permeability differences detected in our inert probe passive diffusion assays and may contribute to the permeability barrier function of the NPC.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Upon co-incubation of recombinant impβ and Nup153FG, large, micron-sized structures formed on a timescale of minutes.
source: Upon co-incubation of recombinant impβ and Nup153FG (the FG domain of Nup153 comprising amino acids 874–1475 [Lim et al., 2006]), large, micron-sized structures formed on a timescale of minutes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When Nup153FG was added to impβ-YFP, large intensity bursts appeared within tens of seconds.
source: However, when Nup153FG (0.5 µM) was added, large intensity bursts appeared within tens of seconds.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The appearance of intensity spikes indicated the formation of large impβ•Nup153 complexes.
source: The appearance of these spikes in intensity (along with their corresponding long tails in the photon counting histograms) indicated the formation of large impβ•Nup153 complexes (Figure 6B,C, red traces).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: These higher-order complexes were orders of magnitude brighter than the freely diffusing impβ-YFP, suggesting that they are comprised of tens or even hundreds of impβ molecules.
source: These higher-order complexes were orders of magnitude brighter than the freely diffusing impβ-YFP, suggesting that they are comprised of tens or even hundreds of impβ molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the brightness of the complexes observed in fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy.

claim: The formation of large complexes can be explained by the many FG motifs found in Nup153's FG domain as well as the multiple sites on impβ's surface that may bind FG repeats.
source: The formation of large complexes can be explained by the many FG motifs found in Nup153's FG domain as well as the multiple sites on impβ's surface that may bind FG repeats.
evidence: This is an inference based on known structural features of Nup153 and impβ.

claim: The addition of RanQ69L•GTP entirely inhibited formation of the impβ•Nup153FG complexes.
source: Notably, the addition of RanQ69L•GTP (2 µM), which does not hydrolyze GTP (Bischoff et al., 1994) and is therefore stably in the GTP-bound form, entirely inhibited formation of the complexes.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: RanQ69L•GTP even dissolved existing large impβ•Nup153FG complexes.
source: RanQ69L•GTP even dissolved existing large impβ•Nup153FG complexes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ran action occurred specifically through impβ (and not Nup153FG) binding since Nup153FG in complex with an impβ truncation lacking the Ran-binding domain, impβ(ΔN70), became insensitive to RanQ69L•GTP.
source: This Ran action occurred specifically through impβ (and not Nup153FG) binding since Nup153FG in complex with an impβ truncation lacking the Ran-binding domain, impβ(ΔN70), became insensitive to RanQ69L•GTP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Large intensity bursts appear with the addition of Nup153FG to TRN1-GFP, indicating the formation of large complexes.
source: Performing similar experiments with TRN1-GFP (100 nM), we again detected spikes in intensity upon addition of Nup153FG, indicating the formation of large complexes (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: RanQ69L•GTP had no observable effect on the TRN1•Nup153FG complexes.
source: However, although TRN1 and RanGTP are known binding partners (Chook and Blobel, 1999), RanQ69L•GTP had no observable effect on the TRN1•Nup153FG complexes, suggesting a functional difference between TRN1 and impβ.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: TRN1-mediated nuclear import is less dependent upon the RanGTP gradient than impβ-mediated import.
source: Indeed, it has been previously reported that TRN1-mediated nuclear import is less dependent upon the RanGTP gradient than impβ-mediated import (Ribbeck et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TRN1 either does not form a meshwork inside the pore or a hypothetical TRN1-mediated barrier has significantly different biophysical characteristics compared to the one formed by impβ.
source: Moreover, the passive diffusion assays (Figure 5E) did not detect alterations of pore permeability in the presence of TRN1, suggesting that TRN1 either does not form a meshwork inside the pore or that a hypothetical TRN1-mediated barrier has significantly different biophysical characteristics (e.g., effective pore size) compared to the one formed by impβ.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that TRN1 does not affect permeability like impβ does.

claim: TRN1 has been shown to bind different sites within the Nup153 FG domain relative to impβ.
source: In support of both those possibilities, TRN1 has been shown to bind different sites within the Nup153 FG domain relative to impβ (Shah and Forbes, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Despite the fact that impβ and TRN1 are both transport receptors and that both can bind Nup153 and form higher-order complexes with it, TRN1 is functionally and biophysically distinct from impβ.
source: Therefore, despite the fact that impβ and TRN1 are both transport receptors and that both can bind Nup153 and form higher-order complexes with it, previous reports (Shah and Forbes, 1998; Ribbeck et al., 1999) and the data shown in Figures 5E, 6D point to TRN1 being functionally and biophysically distinct from impβ.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: There are multiple reports that RanGTP and impβ may have critical additional roles in passive equilibration and active transport.
source: However, there are multiple reports that RanGTP and impβ may have critical additional roles in passive equilibration and active transport.
evidence: This is a summary statement introducing evidence from the literature.

claim: It was proposed that Ran is necessary for impβ-bearing cargos to move past a barrier located at 70 nm along the transport axis.
source: Specifically, it was proposed that Ran is necessary for impβ-bearing cargos to move past a barrier located at 70 nm along the transport axis (Gorlich et al., 1996; Lowe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: We propose the existence of a Ran-sensitive network of interactions between impβ and Nup153 centered at the nuclear face and including the central channel of the NPC, which contributes to the permeability of the pore.
source: Based on the experiments reported here, we propose the existence of a Ran-sensitive network of interactions between impβ and Nup153 centered at the nuclear face and including the central channel of the NPC, which contributes to the permeability of the pore (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of multiple experimental findings.

claim: Nup50 has been shown to promote cargo dissociation from the pore in active transport.
source: Whilst other nuclear basket localized Nups, such as Nup50, have been shown to promote cargo dissociation from the pore in active transport (Sun et al., 2008), Nup153 appears to also have a role in controlling bulk permeability of the NPC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nup153 appears to have a role in controlling bulk permeability of the NPC.
source: Whilst other nuclear basket localized Nups, such as Nup50, have been shown to promote cargo dissociation from the pore in active transport (Sun et al., 2008), Nup153 appears to also have a role in controlling bulk permeability of the NPC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing effects of Nup153 on permeability.

claim: The impβ•Nup153 interaction significantly restricts the ability of inert cargos to diffuse across the NPC, indicating the presence of a non-specific physical barrier that cannot be explained by simple molecular crowding.
source: The impβ•Nup153 interaction significantly restricts the ability of inert cargos to diffuse across the NPC, indicating the presence of a non-specific physical barrier that cannot be explained by simple molecular crowding.
evidence: This is an inference based on passive diffusion assays showing that impβ restricts permeability but TRN1 does not.

claim: This barrier may take the form of a highly cross-linked 'meshwork' of long, flexible Nup153 FG domains fastened to each other by impβ molecules.
source: This barrier may take the form of a highly cross-linked 'meshwork' of long, flexible Nup153 FG domains fastened to each other by impβ molecules, which we characterized in vitro at physiological pH and salt concentrations.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on in vitro complex formation data.

claim: The multiply cross-linked nature of these impβ•Nup153 structures may be reminiscent of the FG gel materials reported by others.
source: The multiply cross-linked nature of these impβ•Nup153 structures may be reminiscent of the FG gel materials reported by others (Frey et al., 2006; Schmidt and Gorlich, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative comparison to previous work.

claim: FG gels are held together by homotypic interactions between the FG domains.
source: However, these FG gels are held together by homotypic interactions between the FG domains; here, materials form via specific coordination between impβ and the FG domains.
evidence: This is a comparison to established knowledge about FG gels.

claim: The impβ•Nup153 material is dynamic, in the sense that its formation and final stability is sensitive to RanGTP.
source: Moreover, the resulting impβ•Nup153 material is dynamic, in the sense that its formation and final stability is sensitive to RanGTP, which can even dissolve existing large impβ•Nup153 complexes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence fluctuation spectroscopy data.

claim: The in vitro fluorescence fluctuation data obtained through spectroscopic studies of purified proteins correlate well with localization microscopy studies of impβ's spatial distribution within the pore.
source: The in vitro fluorescence fluctuation data obtained through spectroscopic studies of purified proteins correlate well with our localization microscopy studies of impβ's spatial distribution within the pore, where we see a sub-population of impβ in the channel that is significantly reorganized by RanGTP.
evidence: This is an inference connecting different experimental approaches.

claim: The photobleach counting experiments suggest that the Ran-sensitive pool is predominantly located at Nup153.
source: Furthermore, the photobleach counting experiments with wild type and reduced Nup153 NPCs suggest that this Ran-sensitive pool is predominantly located at Nup153, although the counting experiments do not rule out other RanGTP-sensitive impβ binding sites within the pore.
evidence: This is an inference based on photobleach counting data comparing wild type and Nup153 knockdown conditions.

claim: The sub-second turnover kinetics of the RanGTP-sensitive impβ pool are similar to kinetic values for impβ turnover inside living cells.
source: The sub-second turnover kinetics of the RanGTP-sensitive impβ pool (Figure 1) are similar to kinetic values for impβ turnover inside living cells (Rabut et al., 2004), suggesting that our reconstituted 'in vitro' permeabilized cell transport assay recapitulates key features of transport in intact living cells.
evidence: This is a comparison to cited literature suggesting physiological relevance of the in vitro system.

claim: On average, 73 ± 16% of impβ molecules in each pore are insensitive to nuclear RanGTP and bound stably to the NPC for many minutes.
source: We estimate that on average, 73 ± 16% of impβ molecules in each pore are insensitive to nuclear RanGTP and bound stably to the NPC for many minutes.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate based on photobleach counting and photo-conversion data.

claim: Impβ is a functional component of the pore and does not just facilitate cargo translocation.
source: These results, coupled with our observation that impβ contributes to the NPC's permeability, suggest that impβ is a functional component of the pore and does not just facilitate cargo translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Other theoretical and experimental studies have suggested that transport receptor binding at the NPC plays a critical role in the non-specific occlusion of inert cargos from entering the pore.
source: Indeed, other theoretical and experimental studies have suggested that transport receptor binding at the NPC plays a critical role in the non-specific occlusion of inert cargos from entering the pore (Zilman et al., 2007; Jovanovic-Talisman et al., 2009; Zilman and Bel, 2010; Schleicher et al., 2014, Kapinos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A functional role of impβ within the NPC is particularly intriguing in light of the structural and functional relationship between karyopherins and scaffold nucleoporins.
source: A functional role of impβ within the NPC is particularly intriguing in light of the structural and functional relationship between karyopherins and scaffold nucleoporins (Andersen et al., 2013; Sampathkumar et al., 2013; Stuwe et al., 2014), suggesting that these two classes of proteins may share a common evolutionary ancestry.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited structural studies.

claim: The bulk of the Ran-insensitive impβ molecules are located near the cytoplasmic face of the pore.
source: At present, we only know (1) that the bulk of these Ran-insensitive impβ molecules are located near the cytoplasmic face of the pore and (2) that they are not bound to Nup153, since reduction of Nup153 (i.e., Δ15370%) did not reduce the impβ counts relative to the RanGTP condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on dSTORM and photobleach counting data.

claim: The Ran-insensitive impβ molecules are not bound to Nup153.
source: At present, we only know (1) that the bulk of these Ran-insensitive impβ molecules are located near the cytoplasmic face of the pore and (2) that they are not bound to Nup153, since reduction of Nup153 (i.e., Δ15370%) did not reduce the impβ counts relative to the RanGTP condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on photobleach counting data comparing Nup153 knockdown with RanGTP conditions.

claim: The single-pore resolution dSTORM and counting experiments revealed significant NPC-to-NPC variation.
source: Although we have emphasized the 'average' characteristics of the NPC vis-à-vis changes in RanGTP levels and other experimental manipulations, the single-pore resolution dSTORM and counting experiments revealed significant NPC-to-NPC variation.
evidence: This is supported by waterfall plots and histograms showing heterogeneity.

claim: The variability of NPC composition may reflect variation of the instantaneous functional state of the cellular pool of several hundred NPCs.
source: The variability of NPC composition may reflect variation of the instantaneous functional state of the cellular pool of several hundred NPCs; perhaps, not all NPCs are functionally equivalent at all times.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed heterogeneity.

claim: The permeability of the NPC, specifically its size-filtering, is sensitive to RanGTP levels.
source: The observation that the permeability of the NPC, specifically its size-filtering, is sensitive to RanGTP levels is interesting in light of recent results that suggest that cells might actively regulate the RanGTP gradient.
evidence: This is supported by passive diffusion assay data.

claim: Cells might actively regulate the RanGTP gradient.
source: The observation that the permeability of the NPC, specifically its size-filtering, is sensitive to RanGTP levels is interesting in light of recent results that suggest that cells might actively regulate the RanGTP gradient.
evidence: This is a statement about recent results in the field.

claim: The RanGTP gradient is generated and maintained by the chromatin-associated RCC1 exchange factor.
source: The RanGTP gradient is generated and maintained by the chromatin-associated RCC1 exchange factor (Bischoff and Ponstingl, 1991) whose activity as well as the local concentration of its RanGDP substrate is subject to multi-tiered regulation (Li and Zheng, 2004; Hood and Clarke, 2007; Yoon et al., 2008; Hitakomate et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: RCC1 activity and the local concentration of its RanGDP substrate is subject to multi-tiered regulation.
source: The RanGTP gradient is generated and maintained by the chromatin-associated RCC1 exchange factor (Bischoff and Ponstingl, 1991) whose activity as well as the local concentration of its RanGDP substrate is subject to multi-tiered regulation (Li and Zheng, 2004; Hood and Clarke, 2007; Yoon et al., 2008; Hitakomate et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The cell might have an extra layer of control over nucleocytoplasmic transport processes by regulating the spatiotemporal characteristics of the RanGTP gradient.
source: Overall, our studies raise the possibility that the cell might have an extra layer of control over nucleocytoplasmic transport processes by regulating the spatiotemporal characteristics of the RanGTP gradient, which would then modulate both the size-cutoff of passive permeability and the extent of active transport.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential cellular regulation mechanisms.

claim: The ability to form the Ran-reversible impβ/Nup153 material in vitro will allow the interplay of energy, impβ, and Ran to be directly investigated.
source: Beyond clarifying the RanGTP-dependent composition and organization of the intact pore, the ability to form the Ran-reversible impβ/Nup153 material in vitro will allow the interplay of energy, impβ, and Ran to be directly investigated and should also allow efficient and selective molecular rectifiers to be created in vitro, not just for biological cargos but also for other substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research possibilities.

claim: The ability to form the Ran-reversible impβ/Nup153 material in vitro should allow efficient and selective molecular rectifiers to be created in vitro.
source: Beyond clarifying the RanGTP-dependent composition and organization of the intact pore, the ability to form the Ran-reversible impβ/Nup153 material in vitro will allow the interplay of energy, impβ, and Ran to be directly investigated and should also allow efficient and selective molecular rectifiers to be created in vitro, not just for biological cargos but also for other substrates.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications.

claim: The optimum impβ concentration for import was ∼1 μM.
source: The optimum concentration was ∼1 μM.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At low impβ concentrations, cargo•impβ complex formation is limited by impβ availability, leading to low import levels.
source: At low impβ concentrations, cargo•impβ complex formation is limited by impβ availability, leading to low import levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At high impβ concentrations, competition for NPC binding sites between free impβ and the cargo•impβ complexes leads to reduced import efficiency.
source: At high impβ concentrations, competition for NPC binding sites between free impβ and the cargo•impβ complexes leads to reduced import efficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: siRNA treatment led to ∼70% protein reduction of Nup153.
source: siRNA treatment led to ∼70% protein reduction of Nup153 (Δ15370%, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Antibody labeling of Nup358/RanBP2 with a second fluorescent dye was used to confirm that the outermost pool of the impβ signal spatially overlapped with the cytoplasmic face of the NPC.
source: Antibody labeling of Nup358/RanBP2 (located on the NPC cytoplasmic filaments) with a second fluorescent dye was used to confirm that the outermost pool of the impβ signal spatially overlapped with the cytoplasmic face of the NPC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by two-color dSTORM data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nup153 is an important terminal binding site for the impβ transport pathway.
source: Nup153 is an important terminal binding site for the impβ transport pathway (Shah et al., 1998; Walther et al., 2001), can bind as many as seven impβ molecules (Milles and Lemke, 2014), and interacts with Ran (Saitoh et al., 1996; Ball and Ullman, 2005; Schrader et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Nup153 can bind as many as seven impβ molecules.
source: Nup153 is an important terminal binding site for the impβ transport pathway (Shah et al., 1998; Walther et al., 2001), can bind as many as seven impβ molecules (Milles and Lemke, 2014), and interacts with Ran (Saitoh et al., 1996; Ball and Ullman, 2005; Schrader et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Nup153 interacts with Ran.
source: Nup153 is an important terminal binding site for the impβ transport pathway (Shah et al., 1998; Walther et al., 2001), can bind as many as seven impβ molecules (Milles and Lemke, 2014), and interacts with Ran (Saitoh et al., 1996; Ball and Ullman, 2005; Schrader et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.
